finding.claim: Broken access control: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result, so any user can overwrite any document body. The sibling handler update_title correctly uses require_edit(), which aborts with 403.
finding.source: PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON body {"body": ...}, sent by any requester with a g.user, including a user who is neither owner nor editor. doc_id is chosen by the attacker.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20 (write to the document store)

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> accepts doc_id from the URL
DOCS[doc_id] loads the document by id with no ownership scoping
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns a bool that is ignored, so there is no abort and no 403
The document body is overwritten with attacker-supplied data

finding.guards_checked: can_edit at line 19 is called but its result is discarded, so it enforces nothing. require_edit (lines 11-13) would abort, but it is not used on this route. Apart from that call, the handler has no other auth or ownership check. The sibling route update_title (line 27) does use require_edit, so it is SAFE. g.user is never set in this file; I assumed external middleware sets it, which is not visible here and is not an authorization check on this resource.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: can_edit (docs.py:7-8) returns a bool that is discarded at docs.py:19; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) aborts 403 but is only used in update_title (docs.py:27). No decorators or before_request hooks in the file.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement with the result ignored, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any authenticated user without an owner/editor check, unlike update_title which uses require_edit at docs.py:27.
